extracted.subtask_description: Use an archive of past NYT Connections puzzles to learn the game's design logic and editor-specific patterns so you can better recognize categories, spot misdirection, and improve solving strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four colour-coded difficulty groups
rubrics_metrics.description: In NYT Connections, you find four groups of four related words, colour-coded by difficulty: Yellow (easiest), Green, Blue, and Purple (hardest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the four groups as an ordered difficulty spectrum: Yellow = easiest / surface-level, Green = slightly harder, Blue = more involved, Purple = hardest. Use the colour as a first heuristic for how deep or tricky the association is likely to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yellow and Green use surface-level associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Yellow and Green categories tend to use surface-level associations, such as types of pasta, dog breeds, things found in a kitchen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect straightforward, concrete groupings (taxonomies, common lists, easily observable attributes) in Yellow/Green; these are often solved by quick pattern recognition and common-category reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blue and Purple require deeper/creative thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blue and Purple categories are where the puzzle gets interesting and, occasionally, ruthless. Purple categories often involve wordplay, cryptic relationships, or obscure references requiring creative thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Blue/Purple look for less-obvious links: wordplay, letter/word transformations, homophones, obscure cultural references, thematic tricks. Allocate more time and lateral-thinking strategies to these groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category titles are often deceptively bland
rubrics_metrics.description: The category title is almost always deceptively bland. “Words that follow FIRE” sounds straightforward but it isn’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a literal or obvious reading of the category title. Treat titles as hints that can mask more inventive or cryptic relationships; re-evaluate literal interpretations if they lead to conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor words can be red herrings
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that seem to anchor an obvious group often belong somewhere else entirely. This is a classic misdirection the editors return to again and again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of immediately obvious anchor words; cross-check other candidate words before committing. Consider alternative groupings and test whether an 'obvious' anchor might serve a trickier theme elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting traps in past puzzles is an effective learning strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Spotting those traps in past puzzles is the fastest way to stop falling into them in future ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively review past puzzles to identify common misdirections and recurring tricks. Use those examples to build an internal checklist of patterns to watch for when solving new puzzles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Browsing the archive reveals puzzle design logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Browsing the archive makes the puzzle’s design logic visible in a way that playing one puzzle a day never quite does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bulk review (multiple puzzles) to surface recurring device types, theme conventions, and editor tendencies that are hard to perceive from isolated play; this reveals the 'why' behind many puzzle constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the editor’s sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The puzzle is edited by crossword constructor Wyna Liu, and her sensibility runs through every past game in this archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning a specific editor’s preferences and recurring devices (by studying many of their puzzles) helps you predict likely tricks and associations; try to 'think the way she thinks' to reduce frustration and increase accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive usage: browse by date and search by word
rubrics_metrics.description: Browse by date to catch up on a puzzle you missed. Search by word if you remember one answer but not the category it belonged to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instructions for using the archive: use chronological browsing to review trends and the search-by-word feature to quickly find where a particular word was used and see its contextual category.
